studies.Reference: Milk, dairy intake and risk of endometrial cancer: a 26-year follow-up.
studies.Authors: Ganmaa D, Cui X, Feskanich D, Hankinson SE, Willett WC
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Milk and dairy consumption were assessed in 1980, 1984, 1986, 1990, 1994, 1998 and 2002 as servings per day

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 68,019 female participants in the Nurses' Health Study
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: The association between total dairy intake and endometrial cancer was significant only among the postmenopausal women
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Milk and dairy consumption were assessed ... as servings per day

studies.Reference: Milk consumption and risk of twelve cancers: A large-scale observational and Mendelian randomisation study.
studies.Authors: Lumsden AL, Mulugeta A, Hyppönen E
studies.Design: Cohort (Mendelian randomisation analysis within UK Biobank)
studies.comparison_type: Continuous (per genetically predicted increase in milk consumption in pre-menopausal females)
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Milk consumption was proxied using a genetic variant (rs4988235) near the lactase gene (LCT) locus.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: white British participants of the UK Biobank (n = up to 255,196)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: greater risk of uterine cancer in pre-menopausal females
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Milk consumption was proxied using a genetic variant (rs4988235) near the lactase gene (LCT) locus.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Insufficient studies to perform formal publication bias testing.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 1.92 (95% CI: 0.96–3.82), indicating no statistically significant association between dairy and uterine cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I² = 74.86%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
